questions.stem: A known patient of Burkitt lymphoma undergoes chemotherapy following which he develops tumor lysis syndrome. All of the following may be seen with tumor lysis syndrome except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypercalcemia

 

  • Tumor lysis syndrome is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic tumors (CLL) and uncommonly solid tumors.
  • It is associated with hypocalcemia and NOT hypercalcemia. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyperuricemia: True. Uric acid levels increase due to the breakdown of nucleic acids released from dying tumor cells.

 

Option B. Hyperkalemia: True. Potassium released from lysed cells causes hyperkalemia, which may lead to cardiac arrhythmias.

 

Option C. Hyperphosphatemia: True. Phosphate released from tumor cells contributes to hyperphosphatemia, which can also result in calcium-phosphate precipitation and renal damage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Tumor lysis syndrome is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic tumors (CLL) and uncommonly solid tumors.
  • It is associated with hypocalcemia and NOT hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male, with a smoking history of 20 pack years, presented in OPD with breathlessness and chest pain. Further investigations revealed a lung tumor. On staining, cells are positive for chromogranin. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Small cell carcinoma

 

The patient presents with clinical features suggestive of a lung tumor, including breathlessness and chest pain. The key diagnostic clue provided is chromogranin positivity in the staining of tumor cells. This is characteristic of small cell carcinoma (SCC), a neuroendocrine tumor commonly associated with smoking history.

 

Additional supporting findings in small cell carcinoma include:

 

  • Presence of neurosecretory granules under electron microscopy.
  • Salt-and-pepper chromatin in the tumor cells observed during histological examination.
  • Basophilic staining of vessel walls (Azzopardi effect) on tissue staining.

 

Small cell carcinoma is strongly associated with smoking and typically presents aggressively, often with paraneoplastic syndromes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adenocarcinoma: Adenocarcinoma of the lung is marked by TTF1 and Napsin A positivity. It often occurs in non-smokers or individuals with lower smoking exposure. This subtype lacks the neuroendocrine markers like chromogranin that are definitive for SCC.

 

Option B. Squamous cell carcinoma: This subtype is linked to markers like P40 and P63, and may present with hypercalcemia or cavitary lesions. Squamous cell carcinoma does not show chromogranin positivity.

 

Option C. Large cell carcinoma: Large cell carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion when other markers are not present. It may occasionally present with paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g., gynecomastia) but is not associated with chromogranin positivity or neurosecretory granules.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The following points about small cell carcinoma:

 

  • Strong association with heavy smoking history.
  • Positive for chromogranin and other neuroendocrine markers.
  • Exhibits neurosecretory granules on electron microscopy and salt-and-pepper chromatin histologically.
  • Aggressive tumor with frequent paraneoplastic syndromes.

questions.stemHtml: A young boy presents to the emergency department with sudden shortness of breath. He also complains of abdominal pain and few episodes of vomiting. In the hospital, he slowly developed a rash on his chest, arms, and legs. His breathing became faster with audible wheezing. On physical examination, he had hypotension and tachycardia. A rash is on his right arm, as shown in the image. After being administered appropriate treatment, the boy improves significantly, and he is able to breathe comfortably. Which of the following is the best marker that could be measured in the serum of this boy to help establish a definitive diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Tryptase

 

The clinical scenario is indicative of anaphylaxis, a severe Type I hypersensitivity reaction. The patient's presentation with sudden shortness of breath, vomiting, wheezing, rash, hypotension, and tachycardia supports this diagnosis. Anaphylaxis involves the release of various mediators, including histamine, from mast cells and basophils.

 

While histamine plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of the reaction, tryptase is considered the best marker for diagnosing anaphylaxis. Tryptase is a protease released specifically by activated mast cells during allergic reactions, and elevated serum levels of tryptase are diagnostic for mast cell activation in anaphylaxis.

 

Key diagnostic clues:

 

  • Sudden onset of respiratory distress and systemic symptoms like vomiting and hypotension.
  • Rash development, which is consistent with urticaria or angioedema.
  • Positive response to adrenaline administration, which is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Prostaglandin D2: Prostaglandin D2 is also released by mast cells during anaphylaxis, contributing to vasodilation and bronchoconstriction. However, it is not routinely measured in clinical practice as a diagnostic marker due to its rapid metabolism and lack of specificity.

 

Option B. Serotonin: Although serotonin may be released in some allergic reactions, its role is more prominent in non-human models of anaphylaxis. It is not specific or sensitive as a diagnostic marker for anaphylaxis in humans.

 

Option C. Histamine: Histamine is a key mediator responsible for the symptoms of anaphylaxis, including wheezing, rash, and hypotension. However, it has a very short half-life in the blood and rapidly metabolizes, making it less reliable than tryptase for diagnostic purposes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Serum tryptase is the most reliable and specific marker for diagnosing anaphylaxis due to its specificity for mast cell activation. Histamine contributes to the symptoms but is not a reliable diagnostic marker due to its short half-life.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with severe flank pain that radiates to the groin. He describes the pain as sudden and excruciating. Laboratory tests reveal hematuria, and imaging shows a 5mm stone located at the ureteropelvic junction of the right kidney. The patient's urine pH is 7.5. Which of the following crystals may be seen in the urine of this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Coffin lid crystals

 

This patient presents with symptoms and findings consistent with urolithiasis (kidney stones). The urine pH of 7.5 suggests an alkaline urine environment, which is characteristic of infection-related stones caused by urease-producing bacteria like Proteus mirabilis. These infections lead to the formation of struvite stones (magnesium ammonium phosphate).

 

  • Coffin lid crystals are the microscopic appearance of struvite crystals in urine. These stones often occur in alkaline urine due to bacterial urease splitting urea into ammonia, leading to an increase in pH.

 

Additional points:

 

  • Struvite stones are commonly associated with staghorn calculi, which can obstruct large portions of the collecting system.
  • The patient's presentation with hematuria, flank pain, and stone visualization is typical for this condition.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rosette shaped crystals: Rosette-shaped crystals are typically associated with uric acid stones, which form in acidic urine (pH < 6). This does not align with the patient’s alkaline urine or clinical findings.

 

Option B. Hexagonal crystals: Hexagonal crystals are indicative of cystine stones, which occur in cystinuria, a rare hereditary condition. These stones are seen in acidic urine and are unrelated to the current case.

 

Option C. Dumb-bell shaped crystals: Dumb-bell shaped crystals are a feature of calcium oxalate monohydrate stones, which are common but usually form in neutral or acidic urine. The patient’s alkaline pH and infection history make this option less likely.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Struvite stones (magnesium ammonium phosphate) form in alkaline urine and are associated with urease-producing bacterial infections (e.g., Proteus). The hallmark urinary crystal for struvite stones is the coffin lid crystal.

questions.stem: Arrange the following steps of platelet changes in the correct sequence during hemostasis:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Platelet adhesion ------platelet activation ----platelet aggregation

 

The sequence of platelet changes during hemostasis occurs as follows:

 

  1. Platelet Adhesion: Platelets first adhere to the exposed subendothelial matrix of the damaged vessel wall. This process is mediated by von Willebrand factor (vWF) binding to glycoprotein 1B (GP1B) on the platelet surface. Adhesion ensures that platelets are localized to the site of injury.
  2. Platelet Activation: Once adhered, platelets are activated by stimuli such as thromboxane A2 (TXA2) and ADP released from the activated platelets. Activation leads to a conformational change in platelets, enhancing their ability to recruit additional platelets and secrete pro-coagulant factors.
  3. Platelet Aggregation: Activated platelets aggregate with each other to form a platelet plug. This process involves fibrinogen binding to glycoprotein 2B3A (GP2B3A) receptors on platelets, linking them together into a cohesive structure.

 

This sequence is critical for the formation of the initial platelet plug, which temporarily seals the vascular injury.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of platelet changes in hemostasis:

 

  1. Adhesion: Mediated by von Willebrand factor and GP1B.
  2. Activation: Stimulated by ADP, thromboxane A2, and other mediators.
  3. Aggregation: Requires fibrinogen and GP2B3A.

 

Additionally, know the disorders associated with defects in these steps:

 

  • Von Willebrand disease: Defect in von Willebrand factor.
  • Bernard-Soulier syndrome: Defect in GP1B.
  • Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia: Defect in GP2B3A.

questions.stem: A pathologist is examining the liver biopsy of a 20-year-old male with cirrhosis. A Prussian blue stain reveals extensive positivity. Laboratory testing does not reveal HbH or Hb Barts. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B)  β-thalassemia major

 

The clinical findings point toward β-thalassemia major for the following reasons:

 

  1. Iron Overload: Prussian blue positivity on the liver biopsy indicates significant iron deposition, which is commonly seen in conditions requiring frequent blood transfusions, such as β-thalassemia major. Transfusions lead to iron overload as the body lacks mechanisms to excrete excess iron.
  2. Absence of HbH and Hb Barts: HbH and Hb Barts are specific for α-thalassemia. Their absence in this case rules out α-thalassemia.
  3. Liver Cirrhosis: Cirrhosis in a young patient with Prussian blue positivity is indicative of long-standing iron overload from transfusions.
  4. Ineffective Erythropoiesis: β-thalassemia major involves a genetic defect in β-globin production, leading to ineffective erythropoiesis. This is characterized by increased bone marrow activity with limited functional red blood cell production, contributing to the need for transfusions.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. α-thalassemia: Ruled out because laboratory findings do not show HbH or Hb Barts, which are hallmark markers of α-thalassemia. Furthermore, α-thalassemia typically does not result in significant iron overload.

 

Option C. Severe iron deficiency anemia: Iron deficiency anemia leads to decreased iron stores, not iron overload. Prussian blue staining would not show positivity, and cirrhosis would not be a finding.

 

Option D. β-thalassemia minor: β-thalassemia minor typically causes mild anemia and does not require transfusions, thus iron overload and cirrhosis are not expected in this condition.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • β-thalassemia major is characterized by iron overload due to repeated blood transfusions.
  • Prussian blue staining identifies iron deposits.
  • Absence of HbH or Hb Barts rules out α-thalassemia.
  • Ineffective erythropoiesis is a hallmark of β-thalassemia major.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient presents with a severe headache, tenderness over the temples, and vision changes, including sudden, painless, and complete loss of vision in one eye. Examination reveals temporal artery tenderness and a palpable, cord-like temporal artery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Giant cell arteritis 

 

The clinical presentation in this case strongly suggests giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis. This condition is a systemic vasculitis that primarily affects the medium and large arteries, particularly the temporal artery.

 

Key clinical features that support the diagnosis:

 

  1. Severe headache and temporal tenderness: These are hallmark symptoms of GCA and are caused by inflammation of the temporal arteries. The palpable, cord-like artery is a characteristic finding.
  2. Vision loss: Sudden, painless, and complete vision loss in one eye is a classic complication of GCA. This results from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to inflammation and occlusion of the ophthalmic or posterior ciliary artery.
  3. Age group: GCA typically occurs in individuals over 50 years of age, with a higher incidence in those aged 70 and older.

 

Diagnosis is often confirmed through:

 

  • Temporal artery biopsy: This reveals granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.
  • Elevated ESR and CRP: Markers of inflammation that are almost universally elevated in GCA.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cluster headache: Cluster headaches present with severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain, often associated with autonomic symptoms (e.g., tearing, nasal congestion). However, they do not cause vision loss or temporal artery tenderness.

 

Option B. Migraine with aura: Migraine with aura may cause visual disturbances such as flashing lights or scotomas. However, sudden and complete vision loss, as well as temporal artery tenderness, are not features of migraines.

 

Option D. Tension headache: Tension headaches cause bilateral, band-like pressure but are not associated with vision changes, temporal artery tenderness, or palpable arterial abnormalities.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a systemic vasculitis affecting individuals >50 years old.
  • Classic symptoms include headache, temporal artery tenderness, and vision loss.
  • Urgent treatment with corticosteroids is critical to prevent bilateral vision loss.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by temporal artery biopsy and elevated ESR/CRP levels.

questions.stem: In case of a FNAC thyroid, which of the following is a standard criteria for calling it as an adequate sample?

options.label: A
options.text: Atleast 10 groups of minimum 6 follicular cells each

options.label: B
options.text: At least 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

options.label: C
options.text: Atleast 3 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

options.label: D
options.text: Atleast 10 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

questions.answerText: At least 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) At least 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

 

The adequacy of thyroid FNAC samples is determined by the presence of an adequate number of follicular cells for cytological analysis. According to accepted guidelines (including the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology), the following is the adequacy criterion:

 

  • At least 6 groups of follicular cells, with each group containing a minimum of 10 well-preserved follicular cells.

 

This ensures there is enough material for a reliable diagnosis while reducing the need for repeat aspirations. If fewer cells or groups are present, the sample is considered nondiagnostic or inadequate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For thyroid FNAC, a sample is adequate if it contains at least 6 groups of follicular cells, with each group having a minimum of 10 cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about “liquid biopsy” in comparison to standard tissue biopsy?

options.label: B
options.text: Can be useful for detection of metastatic subclones of a malignant tumor

options.label: C
options.text: Amount of biological sample is greater in amount

questions.answerText: Amount of biological sample is greater in amount
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Amount of biological sample is greater in amount

 

Liquid biopsies collect smaller amounts of biological material compared to tissue biopsies. This is because liquid biopsy samples often consist of fragments of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) or circulating tumor cells (CTCs), whereas tissue biopsies provide larger samples for extensive analysis. Thus, the statement that the "amount of biological sample is greater" in liquid biopsies is not true.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Easier to perform: This is true because liquid biopsies involve simple procedures like blood draws, avoiding invasive techniques.

 

Option B. Can be useful for detection of metastatic subclones of a malignant tumor: This is true as liquid biopsies can detect circulating tumor cells or DNA from metastatic subclones, aiding in monitoring tumor heterogeneity.

 

Option D. Less invasive: This is true as liquid biopsies are minimally invasive compared to traditional tissue biopsies, which often require surgery or imaging guidance.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Liquid biopsies are easier to perform, less invasive, and useful for detecting metastatic subclones, but the amount of biological sample collected is significantly smaller compared to standard tissue biopsies.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with fatigue, pallor, and frequent nosebleeds. Physical examination reveals petechiae and ecchymoses. Laboratory tests show pancytopenia, with a low hemoglobin level, decreased platelet count, and reduced neutrophil count. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy demonstrate increased blasts (20% of total nucleated cells), and these blasts display Auer rods. Which of the following subtypes of this malignancy indicate a poor prognosis for the patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) AML (therapy related) 

 

AML (therapy-related) is associated with a poor prognosis due to its secondary nature, arising as a complication of prior chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or exposure to alkylating agents or topoisomerase II inhibitors. This subtype has a higher risk of resistance to treatment and shorter survival compared to de novo AML. Therapy-related AML also often involves complex cytogenetic abnormalities.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. AML with multilineage dysplasia: This subtype has an intermediate to poor prognosis, but therapy-related AML generally carries a worse outcome.

 

Option B. AML with recurrent chromosomal translocations: This subtype is associated with a favorable prognosis, especially with specific translocations like t(15;17), t(8;21), and inv(16), as these cases respond well to targeted therapies.

 

Option D. AML (not otherwise classified): This is a broad category that includes AML cases without specific genetic markers or secondary causes. Prognosis varies but is generally better than therapy-related AML.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • AML (therapy-related) has the worst prognosis among AML subtypes due to its resistance to treatment and association with prior chemotherapy or radiation exposure.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about “cell within cell” appearance is not correctly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: Emperipolesis: movement of live cells following internalization

options.label: B
options.text: Efferocytosis: capture and deletion of dying cells by efferocytosis

options.label: C
options.text: Entosis: active internalisation a dead cell into another cell's cytoplasm

options.label: D
options.text: Enclysis: to confine live CD4+ T cells by hepatocytes.

questions.answerText: Entosis: active internalisation a dead cell into another cell's cytoplasm
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Entosis: active internalisation a dead cell into another cell's cytoplasm

 

Entosis refers to the active internalization of a living cell into another cell's cytoplasm, not a dead cell. It is a form of cell cannibalism and is observed in various cancers. This incorrect statement makes it the answer to the question.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Emperipolesis: movement of live cells following internalization: This is correct. Emperipolesis involves the entry of a living cell into another cell without damage, with the possibility of the cell exiting intact.

 

Option B. Efferocytosis: capture and deletion of dying cells by efferocytosis: This is correct. Efferocytosis refers to the clearance of apoptotic cells by phagocytes, involving signals such as phosphatidylserine and complement components (e.g., C1q).

 

Option D. Enclysis: to confine live CD4+ T cells by hepatocytes: This is correct. Enclysis refers to the entrapment of live CD4+ T cells by hepatocytes and has been implicated in autoimmune hepatitis and liver transplant settings.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Entosis: Active internalization of a living cell into another cell's cytoplasm.
  • Emperipolesis: Passage of a live cell through another cell without destruction.
  • Efferocytosis: Clearance of dying cells by phagocytosis.
  • Enclysis: Entrapment of live CD4+ T cells by hepatocytes.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with a painful, swollen neck and fever. Physical examination reveals a tender and enlarged thyroid gland. Laboratory tests show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and thyrotoxicosis with an increased serum concentration of free thyroxine (T4). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis

 

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis) is the most likely diagnosis in this case, as the condition is characterized by:

 

  1. Painful, swollen thyroid gland: A key feature differentiating this condition from other thyroid disorders.
  2. Fever and systemic symptoms: Common in the acute phase.
  3. Elevated ESR: Indicates inflammation, a hallmark of subacute thyroiditis.
  4. Transient thyrotoxicosis: Caused by the release of stored thyroid hormones due to inflammation and destruction of thyroid tissue.

 

This condition is often preceded by a viral infection and resolves spontaneously with symptomatic treatment, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Graves' disease: This is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism but typically presents with a painless goiter and other specific features, such as exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema. It is not associated with a tender thyroid.

 

Option B. Hashimoto's thyroiditis: This is a common cause of hypothyroidism and involves a painless enlargement of the thyroid. It is associated with lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of Hurthle cells, but not with acute pain or elevated ESR.

 

Option D. Toxic multinodular goiter: This condition causes hyperthyroidism due to autonomously functioning thyroid nodules but is not associated with thyroid pain, fever, or elevated ESR.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis): Painful, tender thyroid enlargement with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever) and transient thyrotoxicosis, typically following a viral illness.
